claims.text: The as-synthesized high-entropy alloy has a statistically homogeneous elemental distribution.
The as-synthesized alloy inherently contains nanoscale lattice-strain variations.
The as-synthesized alloy contains subtle local phase fluctuations or minor phase separations.
Controlled annealing can reduce or tailor nanoscale lattice-strain heterogeneity without producing coarse precipitates, secondary phases, or significant grain growth.
A tailored nanoscale distribution of lattice strain and minor phase separations enhances local magnetic-exchange anisotropy.
Enhanced local magnetic-exchange anisotropy produces efficient magneto-structural coupling.
Local strain variations create regions with modified magnetic-exchange interactions.
The strain-modified regions align their magnetic moments more readily under low applied magnetic fields.
Easier low-field moment alignment generates an enhanced magnetocaloric effect.
Maintaining overall microstructural integrity enables rapid heat transfer.
Maintaining overall microstructural integrity preserves mechanical stability.
A distributed rather than abrupt magnetic transition preserves low hysteresis.
Optimally annealed samples will require a lower applied field than the untreated baseline to achieve the same magnetocaloric response.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit increased temperature change or entropy change at low fields relative to the untreated baseline.
Excessive reduction of strain heterogeneity will diminish magnetocaloric performance relative to the optimized state.
The proposed relationship applies only where strain is adjusted without macroscopic phase separation or significant grain growth.

contradictions.description: The prediction explicitly allows excessive strain reduction to worsen magnetocaloric performance, but the falsification rule says that reduced or modified strain failing to improve—or worsening—the response falsifies the mechanism. Without identifying an optimal strain window in advance, an expected over-annealed result could be incorrectly treated as falsification.
